entry.title: Update SAP Table Maintenance Generator (TMG) After Table Structure Changes Without Deleting It
entry.content:
Introduction

In SAP ABAP development, the Table Maintenance Generator (TMG) provides a standard way to maintain table entries through transaction SM30. It allows users to create, modify, and delete records without developing a separate maintenance program.

A common challenge occurs when a new field is added to a custom table that already has a TMG. The updated field may not appear in the existing maintenance screen.

One approach is to delete and recreate the TMG. However, if the existing maintenance dialog contains custom event logic or screen modifications, recreating it can introduce additional rework.

In this blog, we will explore how to update an existing TMG using the generation settings in SAP, without unnecessarily deleting the existing maintenance object.

Prerequisites

Before starting, ensure that:

  • You have an existing custom table with an active TMG.

  • The table is maintained through transaction SM30.

  • You have the required development authorizations.

  • Any existing TMG events or screen modifications have been documented.

Step 1: Check the Existing Table Maintenance Screen

Open transaction SM30 and enter the custom table or maintenance view name.

Choose Maintain to display the current maintenance screen. Note the existing fields and any custom functionality.

Step 2: Add the New Field to the Table

Open transaction SE11 and enter the custom table name.

Choose Change, add the required field to the table definition, maintain its data element and other relevant properties, and activate the table.

If the change requires a database adjustment, assess the impact and perform the necessary adjustment using the appropriate SAP tools and procedures.

Step 3: Open the Existing Table Maintenance Generator

While working with the table in SE11, navigate to:

Utilities → Table Maintenance Generator

Open the existing maintenance generator configuration and choose Change.

The objective is to adjust the existing generated maintenance dialog rather than delete the maintenance object and recreate it from scratch.

Step 4: Select the Appropriate Structure Change Option

In the generation settings, select the option corresponding to the structural change you have made.

For adding a field, select:

New field/sec. table in structure

If a field has been removed, choose the corresponding option for a field or secondary table removed from the structure.

Proceed to the next screen.

Step 5: Review the Field and Screen Settings

Continue through the generation wizard and verify the relevant settings.

Depending on your existing maintenance dialog, confirm:

  • Whether the new field is a key field or a non-key field.

  • Whether the maintenance dialog uses a one-step or two-step layout.

  • Whether the existing screen arrangement remains appropriate.

  • Whether any custom screen changes need to be preserved or reviewed.

Select the options that match your table design and proceed.

Step 6: Complete the Generation Adjustment

Continue through the remaining confirmation screens. Allow SAP to process the changes, then save the updated maintenance configuration.

Check the system messages and resolve any errors before moving to validation.

The exact screens and available options may vary depending on the SAP release and maintenance object configuration.

Step 7: Validate the Changes in SM30

Return to transaction SM30 and open the same table or maintenance view in change mode.

Verify that:

  1. The newly added field is available on the maintenance screen.

  2. Existing fields are displayed correctly.

  3. New and existing records can be maintained as expected.

  4. Relevant custom TMG events continue to behave correctly.

  5. Saving the entries updates the data as intended.

Important Considerations

  • Preserve custom logic: Review existing TMG events and screen modifications before changing generation settings.

  • Validate key changes carefully: Adding or removing key fields can affect maintenance behavior and existing records.

  • Test before transporting: Perform the required functional and regression testing in the development and quality systems.

  • Do not assume every modification is preserved automatically: Custom screen layouts, generated objects, and event implementations should be checked after the adjustment.

Conclusion

When a table structure changes, deleting and recreating the entire Table Maintenance Generator should not be the first option.

By reviewing the existing TMG configuration and selecting the appropriate structure-change settings, you can update the maintenance dialog while reducing unnecessary rework.

Always validate the resulting SM30 screen and existing custom functionality before transporting the changes to another system.

entry.title: CDS Table Entities - Definition of Fields: built-in types and type mappings
entry.content:
The next two parts of the series will dive deeper into field definitions in CDS table entities; this article starting out with ABAP built-in types, and the next focusing on data elements and CDS types. In case you missed the previous post, "Getting Started with CDS Table Entities", you can read it here.

How to define fields in CDS table entities

Table entities are composed of a list of field definitions, all of which follow the structure:

field_definition ::=
    [field_annotation]
    [key] field_name : type_reference [null];

An example field list could look like this:

@ClientHandling.type: #CLIENT_DEPENDENT
@AbapCatalog.deliveryClass: #APPLICATION_DATA
@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'Mountains of the world'
define table entity ZAK_MOUNTAINS
{
  key mountain_id    : abap.raw(16);
      mountain_name  : abap.char(80);
      mountain_range : abap.char(30);
      description    : abap.string null; 
      @Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure: 'height_unit'
      height      : abap.quan(7,2);
      height_unit : abap.unit;      
      first_ascent   : abap.datn; // date of first ascent
      first_ascent_at : abap.utclong; // timestamp of first ascent
      num_routes   : abap.int4;   // known routes to the summit  
      @Semantics.spatialData.srid.value: '0'
      location : abap.geom_ewkb null; 
}

As you can see above, the syntax is still very similar to how fields are defined in classic dictionary tables. Primary key fields are defined with the keyword key, just like one would expect it in classic tables as well.

Fields that contain the keyword null are nullable, meaning these columns may contain SQL null values. Unlike classic tables, CDS table entities officially support nullability. The reason for this is that some datatypes do not have a suitable default value on the database, so they require the null keyword when used in the field definition (a more detailed post on this topic will follow later).

While classic tables contain an explicit client field with type mandt in their field list, CDS table entities handle client dependency implicitly, similarly to CDS view entities. This means that it is no longer necessary to define an explicit client field in the field list. Instead, client dependency is handled via header annotation @ClientHandling.type (more on this will follow in a dedicated article as well). This change in behavior was motivated by two factors: First, aligning the client handling behavior with CDS view entities rather than classic tables leads to more consistency in terms of behavior across different CDS objects. And secondly, since the client field does not contain any true business payload but rather a system-managed key for tenant isolation, it is not necessary to declare it explicitly in the data model.

Numeric types

Let’s start with the easiest kind of datatype: the numeric types. The following numeric built-in types are supported in CDS table entities:

Supported types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.int1

INT1

b (1-byte int)

TINYINT

abap.int2

INT2

s (2-byte int)

SMALLINT

abap.int4

INT4

i (4-byte int)

INTEGER

abap.int8

INT8

int8

BIGINT

abap.dec

DEC

p (packed)

DECIMAL

abap.decfloat16

DECFLOAT16

decfloat16

SMALLDECIMAL

abap.decfloat34

DECFLOAT34

decfloat34

DECIMAL

abap.fltp

FLTP

f (float)

DOUBLE

It should be noted that in classic tables, abap.int1 is mapped to SMALLINT, whereas CDS table entities map this type tp TINYINT. Not only does this save space (which is precious!), it also results in congruent domains in ABAP and the database. This datatype is the only case so far where the type mapping differs between classic tables and CDS table entities.

While abap.dec and abap.decfloat34 are both mapped to DECIMAL on HANA, these two are fundamentally different types with different behavior. The type abap.dec requires two arguments, declaring an explicit length and decimal places via precision (p) and scale (s). The resulting HANA type is therefore a fixed-point DECIMAL(p,s) with hard maximum of p total digits and exactly s fractional digits.
On the other hand, abap.decfloat34 does not have any arguments. It maps to a decimal floating-point number where the precision and scale of the stored value are determined by the value itself. This difference has some practical implications, for example when performing a CAST operation between dec and decfloat34 in CDS.
Similarly, the smaller datatype abap.decfloat16, which is mapped to SMALLDECIMAL, also represents a floating-point decimal. However, unlike abap.decfloat34 which has a capacity of 16 bytes with up to 34 decimal digits, abap.decfloat16 only has a capacity for 8 bytes with up to 16 decimal digits in its coefficient.
Lastly, columns typed as abap.fltp store binary floating-point numbers, meaning only integer powers of 2 can be represented exactly. This can lead to ambiguities and  rounding errors (e.g., after divisions by powers of 10), which is also the reason abap.fltp cannot be used as datatype for key fields in CDS.

Since developing new objects always comes with getting rid of some old pain points from the past, we chose to deprecate some types as well:

Deprecated types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.df16_dec

DF16_DEC

decfloat16

DECIMAL

abap.df16_raw

DF16_RAW

decfloat16

VARBINARY

abap.df16_scl

DF16_SCL

decfloat16

VARBINARY

abap.df34_dec

DF34_DEC

decfloat34

DECIMAL

abap.df34_raw

DF34_RAW

decfloat34

VARBINARY

abap.df34_scl

DF34_SCL

decfloat34

VARBINARY

abap.prec

PREC

s (2-byte int)

NVARCHAR

While types DF16_DEC and DF34_DEC (decimal floating point stored in binary coded decimal format) can be changed to type DEC without adjustments on the database, DF16_RAW and DF34_RAW (stored in binary format) require a table conversion to be changed to DEC or DECFLOAT16 or DECFLOAT34, respectively. DF16_SCL and DF34_SCL (stored in binary format with specific scaling) as well as PREC are officially obsolete. Since HANA has native built-in decfloat support, the old decfloat types listed above are no longer needed and therefore deprecated.

Character-like types

The following character-like types are supported as well:

Supported types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.char

CHAR

c

NVARCHAR

abap.string

STRG

string

NCLOB

abap.sstring

SSTR

string

NVARCHAR

abap.numc

NUMC

n

NVARCHAR

abap.lang

LANG

c

NVARCHAR

In CDS table entites, abap.string will no longer have a length component besides abap.string(0) (a length of zero means „unlimited length“). This means we always consider strings to have no length limits. An important distinction however is that "no length limit" does not mean "infinite storage". It simply means that the type itself does not impose a limit to how long a string value can be. The underlying NCLOB column in the database still has a physical ceiling which belongs to the infrastructure layer.
Due to the lack of suitable default values for NCLOBS on the database, abap.string is also denoted as a nullable type, i.e., it is one of the datatypes which require the null keyword (along with abap.rawstring, see below). Not adding this keyword will result in syntax errors.
Unlike abap.string, abap.sstring can also be used in where clauses, join conditions and indices.

Can‘t we just use NUMC for every number? – Our recommendations

The datatype abap.numc is one of the most frequently used types, e.g. to denote different kinds of IDs such as buyer IDs or item numbers. It is a character-like type that accepts only digits, and maps to NVARCHAR on the database just like any other CHAR-like type. Since abap.numc is digit-only and auto-pads with leading zeros, it appears more controlled at handling numbers than a plain CHARat first glance. However, it lacks all of the actual semantics of numeric types (such as arithmetic, ordering, or range checks). Overusing abap.numc can therefore lead to potential problems:

  • Since NUMC is a character-like type on the database, SQL aggregations such as AVG, SUM or MAX cannot be used on NUMC-fields. Moreover, there isn’t any digit-only enforcement on the database either: In the old dynpro world, screen field validation would at least catch non-digit input at the UI layer, however, In a RAP/Fiori Elements world, that enforcement is gone unless you explicitly add a validation in the behavior definition.
  • Comparisons with other CHAR-fields may lead to unexpected results due to implicit conversion rules if the CHAR-field is not purely numeric (e. g., in where-clauses).
  • NUMC-fields of different lengths are not cast-compatible (e. g. abap.numc(5) and abap.numc(6)), resulting in errors when attempting to join similar looking „numbers“ across different entities.
  • NUMC is only compatible with CHAR and other NUMC fields of equal or greater length in comparisons and ON-conditions. For example, defining a NUMC key in a child entity and attempting to join it to a parent which contains a NUMC-field of a different length will result in an activation error. It can only be fixed by realigning lengths, which may even require a table migration if the table already contains data.
  • Using NUMC in Native SQL and AMDP is explicitly discouraged in the docs, as conversions in the Native SQL interface should be avoided whenever possible.
  • NUMC fields in OData services typically need explicit handling to avoid the leading zeros being stripped, or the field being mistyped on the consumer side.

There is a legitimate use case for abap.numc though, which is whenever there are fixed-length numeric identifiers where leading zeros are part of the business meaning (e.g., as item or order numbers). For other use cases, we recommend the following:

  • For technical primary key fields, you can use the data element UUID for example (which has base type RAW(16)) rather than NUMC. UUID keys enable managed early numbering, meaning the RAP framework generates them automatically in the BDEF and no custom numbering logic is needed. In unmanaged BOs or classic ABAP, UUIDs can be generated via CL_SYSTEM_UUID directly, while in ABAP Cloud/BTP you can use the XCO library as well.
  • For counters or internal sequences, actual numeric types such as abap.int4 should be used instead.
  • For fiscal years or posting periods, we recommend using a DATN column instead. If for some reason this is not possible, the more suitable alternative would be using dedicated data elements or CDS types which have NUMC as their base type, but feature proper conversion exits as well. For data elements they can be directly included in the domain, while in CDS types they are added via annotation AbapCatalog.typeSpec.conversionExit.
  • For digit sequences such as postal codes, abap.char is the more future-proof choice in case letters need to be added later.
  • Any field which is exposed in OData should have also a CHAR-type instead of NUMC to avoid the need for extra handling of the leading zeros.

Lastly, some character-like types are also no longer supported in CDS table entities:

Deprecated types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.lchr

LCHR

c

NVARCHAR if length < 5000, else NCLOB

abap.varc

VARC

string

NVARCHAR or BLOB

abap.clnt

CLNT

c

NVARCHAR

The type abap.clnt is known for being used solely for client fields. However, since we no longer denote client fields explicitly, we chose to no longer support this type either to avoid confusion.

The issue with abap.lchr is that this type requires the field length to be declared as an additional INT-field right before the LCHR, which is already impractical. Additionally, there can be only one such LCHR field in a table, and both the INT- and LCHR fields have to be the last columns at the end of the table. Since this type has no advantages on the database, we recommend using abap.string or abap.sstring instead, which map to proper LOB column types in HANA and get the job done just as well.


Byte-like types

With regards to byte-like types, the following are supported in CDS table entities:

Supported types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.raw

RAW

x

VARBINARY

abap.rawstring

RSTR

xstring

BLOB

The type abap.rawstring, just like abap.string, is also considered to have unlimited length and has no allowed length component other than abap.rawstring(0). Moreover, it is nullable as well, requiring the null keyword.

The type abap.lraw however is deprecated, since it poses a similar problem as abap.lchr. It can be replaced in the same fashion with abap.raw or abap.rawstring.

Deprecated types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.lraw

LRAW

x

VARBINARY if length <= 1000, else BLOB


Currency and quantity types

One of the most frequent use cases is denoting currency and quantity fields. All the currency and quantity types you are already familiar with are supported in CDS table entities and mapped as follows:

Supported types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.curr

CURR

p

DECIMAL

abap.cuky

CUKY

c

NVARCHAR

abap.quan

QUAN

p

DECIMAL

abap.unit

UNIT

c

NVARCHAR

The element annotations @Semantics.amount and @Semantics.quantity  are of course still mandatory when using abap.curr and abap.quan respectively, since activation will fail without them.


Date and time

For date and time formats, we decided to only support the more modern types abap.datn, abap.timn and abap.utclong/abap.utcl, while deprecating the „old“ types abap.dats, abap.tims and abap.accp. An overview can be seen below:

Supported types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.datn

DATN

d

DATE

abap.timn

TIMN

t

TIME

abap.utclong

UTCLONG

utclong

TIMESTAMP

Deprecated types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.dats

DATS

d

NVARCHAR

abap.tims

TIMS

t

NVARCHAR

abap.accp

ACCP

n

NVARCHAR

This change mainly stems from architectural reasons: the old types are character-like formats with ABAP-specific semantics that don't cleanly translate to proper database column types. A DATS-field simply contains a character in format 'YYYYMMDD', but the values are not enforced. A DATN-field on the other hand contains a true DATE-type value, meaning the column is enforced to have a valid date on the database. A similar principle can be applied to TIMS/TIMN: while TIMS is mapped to NVARCHAR, TIMN represents a true time value on the database as well. One example use case where this comes in handy is when calculating date and time directly on the database within an AMDP procedure. CDS table entities are designed to have real, native database columns, so therefore the old character-like types are no longer supported.

What time is it, actually? - Some remarks on time zones and timestamp conversions

A lot of users are still familiar with the legacy conversion functions CONVERT_DATE_TO_TIMESTAMP, GET_CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, etc. These functions combine the system date and time (sy-datum and sy-uzeit) and reconstruct a timestamp in UTC format. This is a common pitfall, since the resulting value does not represent the time in the „true“ UTC time zone, but instead the local system time in the respective „utclong“ format. The built-in type abap.utclong on the other hand maps to a real HANA TIMESTAMP column, meaning HANA's own SQL timestamp functions (ADD_SECONDS, SECONDS_BETWEEN, etc.) work directly on it without format conversion overhead. Furthermore, the UTCL_* family of CDS functions (UTCL_CURRENT, UTCL_ADD_SECONDS, UTCL_SECONDS_BETWEEN) only work on utclong-typed fields, whereas the older TSTMP_* functions only work on TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPL (which are data elements with base type decimal).

There is one very practical question that still remains here: if a user wants to store an event time, should they use UTCLONG alone, or DATN+TIMN+UTCLONG?

Our recommendation is to use utclong as the primary timestamp. DATN and TIMN are for cases where the date or time-of-day alone has independent business meaning. We also strongly discourage reconstructing timestamps from date and time in the same way it had been done with dats and tims in the past. Timestamps are stored in UTC, and recreating this antipattern would lose the time zone safety in the process.


Geodata types

The HANA type ST_GEOMETRY, which is used to store geometric data in EWKB representation, is supported in both classic tables and CDS table entities via the type abap.geom_ewkb:

Supported types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.geom_ewkb

GEOM_EWKB

xstring

ST_GEOMETRY

This type has some special properties: it has no length, and it requires the specification of spatial reference system identifier (SRS ID or SRID). A spatial reference system defines the coordinate framework used to describe positions on earth, e.g., specifying the origin point, axis directions and units of measurement. The SRID is set via the field annotation AbapCatalog.geo.spatialRefSystem: '<SRID>, the default value being SRID=0. With a given SRS ID for a geodata column, the SRS ID is fixed at table creation. All records need to have this SRS ID, and it cannot be changed later. 
For CDS table entities on particular, we officially support SRID = NULL, which also changes the behavior compared to classic tables. If NULL is set as SRID, the SRS is not fixed at table creation anymore, meaning different values can be inserted later. This option however comes at the expense of performance. Furthermore, this type cannot be used for key fields regardless of whether the SRID is NULL or not.
Just like abap.string and abap.rawstring, abap.geom.ewkb is a nullable type and requires the null keyword as well.

This already concludes the first part on field definitions, builtin-types and type mappings. The next part of this series is going to cover data elements, CDS simple types and enumerations, so stay tuned!

entry.title: Working on SAP ECC-to-S/4HANA Remediation as a Functional Consultant with KTern.AI CodeGenie
entry.content:
Why the Remediation Was Needed

During a SAP remediation project, I worked on custom ABAP program analysis and remediation with the help of KTern.AI CodeGenie.

The remediation was triggered by an organizational-structure reassignment in the client's environment. Several custom programs relied on hard-coded organizational values, which needed to be addressed as part of the change.

Instead of simply replacing the old values with new hard-coded values, the project used a custom Z table. The program name and an ID were used to identify the relevant variable, and its value was maintained in the table. The program could then retrieve the required value instead of relying on a value embedded directly in the source code.

This approach made the remediation more maintainable because future changes to the relevant values could be handled through table maintenance rather than requiring another source-code modification for every affected value.

What made this project particularly interesting to me was my role. I was working as a SAP functional consultant, but the remediation required me to investigate technical issues, understand ABAP programs, and work with code changes. This was where CodeGenie became particularly useful.

Setting Up KTern.AI CodeGenie in VS Code

We used KTern.AI CodeGenie through Visual Studio Code. The setup involved installing the relevant KTern extensions, configuring an MCP server to connect to the SAP system, and adding the custom-code remediation skill required for the work.

Once the connection and skill were configured, we could interact with CodeGenie using natural language. We could ask it to retrieve and explain source code, trace program execution, identify relevant database tables, and investigate specific issues.

Another detail I noticed was that CodeGenie created a dedicated folder for each chat. This helped keep the artifacts associated with individual sessions organized.

How I Used CodeGenie as a Functional Consultant

As a functional consultant, I am more accustomed to working with business processes, configuration, master data, and functional issues than to spending all my time analyzing ABAP code.

During this project, I needed to understand existing custom programs, investigate why certain reports were failing, identify dependencies, and work through technical remediation.

CodeGenie helped bridge the gap between functional understanding and technical implementation.

For example, I could ask it to explain the purpose of a program, identify the tables it used, trace the execution flow, and explain how different parts of the code worked together. When an error occurred, I could ask it to investigate the underlying cause instead of relying only on the error message.

When a code change was required, I could discuss the intended behavior with CodeGenie, clarify the expected flow, and review the updated code it generated.

This made working on technical remediation much more approachable for me as a functional consultant. It did not eliminate the need to understand the business process or validate the changes, but it made technical investigation easier and helped me work more confidently with custom ABAP programs.

Working Through Several SAP Programs Over a Couple of Months

Across seven sessions spanning a couple of months, I used CodeGenie to investigate and work with several custom SAP programs. These covered purchasing, pricing, GST reporting, physical inventory, warehouse management, scheduling agreements, and BOM reporting.

The programs had different purposes and levels of complexity. Some generated reports, while others uploaded data or updated business documents.

Rather than listing every program individually, I want to highlight the types of work CodeGenie helped me with.

Understanding Existing Program Logic

Some programs contained multiple includes, custom function modules, or class dependencies. Understanding the complete execution flow required looking beyond a single source file.

CodeGenie retrieved and analyzed the source and helped explain how the different components worked together. It traced flows such as file upload, input validation, authorization checks, database updates, and ALV output generation.

For a GST sales register, it also helped explain the output columns and how the report handled different tax types and special business scenarios.

This was useful because understanding what an existing program was doing was an important first step before deciding what needed to change.

Understanding Existing Technical Changes

The programs contained various technical changes and dependencies that needed to be understood before further remediation.

CodeGenie helped explain database access patterns, replacements involving CDS views and compatibility views, and the handling of hard-coded values.

For me, this made it easier to understand the existing implementation and identify the areas that needed further investigation.

A Practical Example: Remediating a Cycle Count Report

One of the clearest examples from my experience involved a cycle count overview report that consolidated physical inventory information from Materials Management (MM) and Warehouse Management (WM).

During testing, we encountered an issue related to the fiscal year variant. A value was hard-coded in the program, but that value was not configured for the relevant year in the test system.

CodeGenie helped investigate the issue and presented two possible approaches: correcting the SAP configuration or changing the code. We chose the code-remediation approach.

CodeGenie investigated the relationship between the plant, valuation area, company code, and fiscal year variant. It also queried the live SAP system to verify the relevant values.

After checking the lookup chain, the remediation replaced five hard-coded fiscal year variant literals with dynamic derivation.

The change was then applied under a transport request, with the relevant locking, activation, and system-update steps.

What I found valuable was the investigation that happened before the code change. The issue was not approached simply as a request to replace a hard-coded value. The relevant organizational relationships and system values were examined to determine how the program should derive the required value.

As a functional consultant, this was a useful example of how I could participate in technical remediation with support from an AI coding agent while still reviewing the proposed solution.

Code Changes Were Only One Part of the Work

The development workflow involved more than asking CodeGenie to rewrite a program.

We first identified an object flagged as requiring remediation. We then asked CodeGenie to analyze the program and explain the issue. Once we understood the existing flow, we discussed the required changes and clarified the intended behavior.

CodeGenie could then make the proposed changes and display the updated code for review.

We checked whether the code contained all the changes discussed and whether the implementation matched the intended approach. If we were satisfied, we could approve the changes and have CodeGenie push the code to the SAP system through a transport request (TR).

This review step was important. We did not simply accept every generated change without checking it. We needed to understand the requirement and confirm that the proposed implementation reflected what had been agreed.

The workflow helped connect program analysis, code changes, review, and transport handling in one process.

Testing: Finding the Right Data Was Not Always Easy

One of the biggest practical challenges was finding suitable test data.

CodeGenie could suggest test cases and query the SAP system for relevant data. However, the first suggested test cases did not always produce the expected output. In some cases, executing the program returned no data.

When this happened, we asked CodeGenie to investigate possible master-data and configuration issues. Through multiple exchanges, we eventually identified working test data for the scenarios we were investigating.

Some of the issues encountered included:

  • Customer-material information records missing from the test system.

  • No suitable bills of material available for the selected materials.

  • Sales organizations in the test system differing from those used in production.

  • Configuration combinations missing from custom configuration tables.

  • Selection-screen parameters preventing the expected BOM from being found.

  • Missing descriptions in master data resulting in blank fields in exported output.

These issues highlighted an important distinction between changing code and validating its behavior. Even when the program logic is understood, testing can depend on suitable master data, configuration, organizational assignments, and input values.

For example, while testing a BOM explosion report, the BOM Application selection parameter contributed to a NO_SUITABLE_BOM_FOUND error. Clearing that field allowed the program to execute successfully and generate the expected CSV output. Reviewing the result also revealed a missing OEM device description in the relevant master data.

This was a useful reminder that successful execution does not automatically mean the output is complete or correct.

CodeGenie helped us investigate these issues, but the process was iterative. Its initial test suggestions were not always sufficient, and we had to ask further questions and investigate the underlying data and configuration before arriving at a working scenario.

For me, this was an important practical lesson: AI-assisted testing still requires careful investigation when the test environment does not contain the data or configuration needed for a scenario.

No-Data Issues and Variant Remediation

Apart from source-code remediation, the work also involved investigating reports that returned no data and programs whose variants did not produce the expected results.

A no-data issue occurs when a report is expected to return output based on available master data, but execution produces an empty screen or no results. The challenge is to determine whether the cause lies in the program logic, selection criteria, master data, configuration, or another dependency.

Variants introduce a related challenge. A program may execute successfully, but a particular variant may not retrieve the expected data. The variant and the way its selection parameters interact with the underlying program logic need to be investigated.

CodeGenie helped us analyze the program behavior and investigate these issues. As with the testing examples, reaching the correct conclusion sometimes required multiple exchanges and checking the available system data.

These scenarios reinforced that remediation is not always about syntax or replacing a hard-coded value. Understanding why a program does not return the expected result is often just as important as making the code change itself.

What I Took Away from the Experience

Across these sessions, I found CodeGenie useful for several connected activities:

  • Understanding existing ABAP programs and their execution flows.

  • Investigating code dependencies across includes, function modules, and classes.

  • Understanding existing technical changes and hard-coded values.

  • Querying SAP data to investigate errors and identify suitable test data.

  • Finding potential master-data and configuration gaps.

  • Implementing agreed code changes and supporting the review and transport workflow.

The most important benefit for me was how it helped me approach technical remediation as a functional consultant. I could use my understanding of the business process and SAP functionality while relying on CodeGenie to help investigate the technical implementation.

At the same time, the experience showed that AI assistance does not eliminate the need for technical judgment. The requirements still need to be clear, code changes need to be reviewed, and unsuccessful tests need to be investigated rather than assumed to be correct.

The most effective workflow was not simply asking CodeGenie to fix a program. It was using it to understand the issue, discuss the required approach, investigate relevant SAP data, review the resulting changes, and work through testing problems until we could identify a suitable scenario.

For SAP functional consultants who need to work with custom ABAP programs, this kind of assistance can make technical remediation more approachable.

My main takeaway is that KTern.AI CodeGenie can be a useful partner in SAP remediation—not as a replacement for functional knowledge or human review, but as a tool that helps connect functional understanding with technical investigation and implementation.

entry.title: Changelog for SAP objects - Verify clean core level C compliance of your custom extensions
entry.content:
In the clean core level concept outlined in the Clean core extensibility for SAP S/4HANA Cloud whitepaper, custom extensions using arbitrary SAP internal objects can be qualified as conditional clean core Level C extensions if dedicated pre‑upgrade checks based on changelog for SAP objects are executed for these extensions.

 Internal SAP objects can change at any point in time during an upgrade. Incompatible changes include, for example, deletion of objects, renaming or deletion of parameters or methods and others.

 To detect in custom code the usage of SAP internal objects, which have been incompatibly changed, SAP now provides the changelog for SAP objects, which contains the names of all SAP standard objects (and their associated components like methods or parameters), that have undergone incompatible changes in the new release. Technically, the changelog information is transferred via the Simplification Database infrastructure from the SAP Support Portal to your system. You can download it from the SAP Software Download Center of the SAP Support Portal and import it into your ABAP test cockpit (ATC) check system.

The changelog information is integrated and considered in the clean core ATC check Usage of APIs which can then detect in custom code the use of SAP objects and their associated components (sub-objects), that have been incompatibly changed.  

 SAP recommendation is to consider changelog during regular ATC quality checks to identify, early in the development process, any usages in custom code of SAP internal objects that have undergone incompatible changes. The changelog information should be included in the ATC check at the latest before the system upgrade, following the same approach as for the ATC checks related to the SAP S/4HANA simplification items.

 This will help to better estimate the risk of custom code not functioning properly after the next release upgrade.

Current functional scope

 The changelog provides information of incompatible changes affecting SAP APIs classified as released API, classic API, or internal API.

It focuses on the deletion of SAP development objects and their associated components (sub-objects) for the following object types:

  • Classes
  • Interfaces
  • Function modules
  • CDS views (DDLS)

 Deletions are reported as warnings for both the affected objects and their sub-objects. These include methods, attributes, types, method and function module parameters, and CDS view fields.

 The current changelog version covers deletions introduced during upgrades from SAP S/4HANA 2023 to SAP S/4HANA 2025, helping developers identify potentially incompatible changes in SAP development objects and assess their impact on custom code.

Prerequisites

In your SAP S/4HANA 2023 or later system (private cloud or on-premise)  you are adopting the clean core level concept outlined in the Clean core extensibility for SAP S/4HANA Cloud whitepaper and following the ABAP test cockpit (ATC) recommendations for governance of clean core ABAP development. You have already configured the Usage of APIs clean core check in your ATC system.

Setup

First download the changelog with the Simplification Database (SAP Note 3693326 (part 1)). As a result, the changelog.zip file is downloaded to your drive.

Next to enable the changelog functionality implement the relevant SAP Note 3758771 - Changelog Support in Usage of API ATC check.

Once the SAP Note has been implemented, upload the changelog content to the system in which the ATC check runs.

  • Remote ATC setup: Upload the changelog content to the central ATC check system.
  • Local ATC setup: Upload the changelog content to the local ATC system.

 PLEASE NOTE: If you are already using ATC on SAP BTP as your central ATC check system for your systems landscape, you can upload and use the changelog in your local SAP S/4HANA 2023 system, as the changelog functionality is not yet available in ATC on SAP BTP.

 To upload the changelog content on your ATC system go to the ABAP Editor (SE38) and execute the SYCM_API_CLASSIFICATION_MANAGR program (F8):

Click on the button Upload API File (Ctrl + F3), choose "Changelog" as a file type in the popup dialog and click on the Confirm. Select the previously downloaded changelog.zip file from your drive.

Once you see the uploaded file with data type "Changelog" in the Data Sources overview, the changelog is active and will report findings when running the ATC check "Usage of APIs".

NOTE: Only one file of the data type "Changelog" can exist in the Data Sources overview. To update the changelog, first delete the existing file, then upload a new version by following the steps described above.

How to use changelog in a pre-upgrade scenario

Execute an ATC run using any check variant containing the Usage Of APIs ATC check over your custom code in the system. In the list of ATC findings, you will see the issues related to the changelog, clearly recognizable from the Check Message text:

In the details of a changelog related ATC finding, you will see more information regarding your incompatibility issue reported by the changelog:

How to use changelog during development

It is recommended to consider changelog also during your development process. For this purpose your ATC check variant, used during development process, must contain the Usage of APIs check along with the changelog information.

In this example ABAP_CLOUD_DEVELOPMENT check variant is used in the development system, and the Usage of APIs check considers the changelog information. The changelog related ATC findings will be displayed with detailed check messages in the ATC result:

What’s next

Support for the changelog in ATC on SAP BTP is already on the short-term roadmap. The changelog approach for SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS levels and future SAP S/4HANA versions will be communicated soon.

entry.title: SAP BASIS HEALTH CHECK COCKPIT – ONE ABAP REPORT (NO SOLMAN / NO CALM)
entry.content:
Hello everyone,

It has been a long time since my last blog post. Work kept me busy, and honestly I only wanted to come back with something new, something that's not already on the community and that can really save time for others. I don't like repetitive work, and I don't like writing about things that already have ten blog posts. So here I am with a new one.

All my earlier blog posts were on Basis technical topics. This is my first blog post with ABAP . As a Basis person I'm not a full-time developer, but this need came straight from my daily work, so I decided to build it myself.

In this blog post we will learn:

  • How a Basis team can do active daily monitoring without SAP Solution Manager, SAP Cloud ALM or any other monitoring tool
  • How one ABAP report checks around 28 areas (application server, HANA DB, security, transport, interfaces and mail) in one run
  • How red / yellow / green colors help you see problems straight away
  • The prerequisites (2 Z-tables plus indexes) and the full source code, ready to copy

Here is the trailer, for full picture scroll down 🙃

THE PROBLEM – WHY I BUILT THIS:

Many landscapes, especially small and mid-size customers, do not have SolMan or CALM connected. Sometimes it's licence, sometimes the project is "still planned", sometimes nobody owns it. But the business still expects the Basis team to know about a problem before users call.

So what do we do? Every morning we open the same transactions, one by one:

SM51 → SM50 → SM66 → ST22 → SM37 → SM13 → SM12 → SP01 → SMLG → ST06 → DBACOCKPIT → STRUST → SCC4 → SE06 → STMS → SM58 → SMQ1 → SMQ2 → SOST …

and then the same again for the next system.

In my experience this takes [30–45] minutes per system if everything is fine, and more if something is not. After some days the eyes get used to the screens and small things get missed: one cancelled job, one SYSFAIL queue, a certificate expiring in 25 days. That is exactly what comes back later as a P1 ticket.

I wanted one screen that tells me what's wrong, how bad it is, and where to click to fix it.

WHAT THE REPORT DOES:

The report is ZBC_HEALTH_COCKPIT. In simple words:

  1. You pick a time window (since last run, today, yesterday, last N hours or a date/time range).
  2. The report runs all selected checks and gives each finding a severity.
  3. You get a summary ALV, one row per check, with the worst issues on top.
  4. Double-click a row → detail ALV with every finding for that check.
  5. Double-click a detail row → it jumps straight to the transaction (SM37, ST22, SMQ2, STRUST …), with authority check.
  6. Results are saved to history, and old runs are deleted automatically after N days (minimum 7).

SEVERITY AND COLOURS:

Severity Color Meaning
CRITICAL 🔴 RedAct now
HIGH🟠 OrangeAct today
WARNING🟡 YellowKeep an eye on it
INFO 🔵 BlueInformation only
OK🟢 GreenAll good
NOT CHECKED ⚪ GreyCheck could not run (authorization, connection…). Never shown as green.

That last point matters to me. If a check fails, it should never look green. A false green is worse than no monitoring at all.

CHECKS COVERED:

Area Checks
Application serverSM51 servers up/ping, SM50 free DIA/BTC/UPD WPs %, SM66 long-running WPs, ST22 dumps (with top runtime errors), SM37 cancelled jobs, SM13 update errors, SM12 old locks, spool number range %, SMLG logon group reachability/response, ST06 OS CPU / RAM / swap / disk I/O
Database (SAP HANA)Current and historical HANA alerts, data/log backup age (log_mode aware), memory vs allocation limit, CPU, disk volumes, services
Security & transportSSL certificate expiry (via standard report SSF_ALERT_CERTEXPIRE), SCC4 client open/closed, SE06 system/namespace change option, STMS imports with RC 4 / RC 8+
Interfaces & mailSM58 tRFC errors, SMQ1 / SMQ2 queues in error/stop, SOST failed/waiting mails

Every threshold (Warn / High / Critical) can be set on the selection screen, so you can save one variant for PRD and a different one for QAS/DEV.

1st screen of the report: where pre-select data will be there and also can be change based on your requirement keep last run reason as we have table too to store the data so not need to worry much but based on requirement you can select the options.

as there are multiple screens, every area param can be selected from each tab.

every tab have options, where you can change or update the values based on requirement and save it as variant, coz every landscape is having different requirement so instead of static i kept it dynamic so no code change needed only screen value is sufficient.

once executed it will show the top level ALV, where we can doubleclick on line item to see the details, if click on tcode it will route you tcode screen also

and in detail while click on that line item it will be easy to navigate and show the error information like below for each

every section and its details, a ease of life for monitoring team 😎

HOW THIS HELPS IN DAILY LIFE:

  • Time saving: my morning check went from [30–45] minutes to about [2–5] minutes per system. Run it, look at the red and orange rows, double-click, fix.
  • Better eye attention: we humans spot red much faster than a number in a column. Problems jump out of the screen.
  • Nothing gets skipped: on a busy day it's tempting to skip "just SOST" or "just STRUST". The report never skips.
  • Background job friendly: schedule it in SM36 with a variant (e.g. every 2–4 hours). With "Since last successful run" each run only looks at what's new since the previous one, so there's no overlap and no gap.
  • History for audits and handover: results stay in Z-tables, so you can show "what was the system status last Tuesday at 08:00".
  • Same standard for the whole team: a junior colleague and a senior colleague look at the same checks and the same thresholds.

A BIG THANK YOU:

This development would not have been possible without my friend i cannot disclose his/her name, who gave me access to his/her system to build and test it. A monitoring report can't be tested properly on a blank sandbox; you need real dumps, real jobs, a real HANA. Thank you, my friend, for the trust and the support. 🙏

I intentionally add his/her so no one in network also able to guess his/her name, it's a tricky part for my mates 😋

here is the code and other prerequisite ( in hindi we can say real masala 😅)

PRE-REQUISITES:

# Requirement
1SAP_BASIS 7.50 or higher (the code uses new Open SQL syntax and inline declarations). Built and tested on SAP S/4HANA on SAP HANA.
2Two Z-tables, ZBC_HC_RUN and ZBC_HC_RES: mandatory, see below
3Secondary indexes on ZBC_HC_RUN, so "since last run" and housekeeping stay fast
4SAPOSCOL running on all hosts (for the ST06 check)
5For the HANA checks, the DB user needs read access to SYS monitoring views and _SYS_STATISTICS (e.g. the MONITORING role). If your default connection user doesn't have it, create a DBCO connection with a monitoring user and enter it in the "HANA DB connection" field.
6Authorizations for the user / background job user to read the relevant admin data (SM50/SM51/SM12/ST22 etc.) and to call the jump-to transactions

TABLE 1: ZBC_HC_RUN (RUN HEADER)

INDEXES (FOR FASTER RUNS):

ZBC_HC_RES(primary key)MANDT, RUN_ID, SEQNODetail reads and deletes by RUN_ID already use the primary key, so no extra index is needed
 
 
CONCLUSION:
Proactive Basis monitoring does not require complex monitoring infrastructure. By consolidating critical checks into one ABAP report with direct drill-down capability, teams can **reduce daily check routines from 45 minutes to under 5 minutes**.
